lines.text: Two countries share this island.
Every six months, one hands it to the other.
So who owns it?
It sits in the Bidasoa river, between Hendaye in France and Irun in Spain.
In 1659, France and Spain ended a war that began in 1635.
They signed the peace on this island, on the seventh of November.
But nobody could fix the border through the river. Commissioners tried for almost two centuries.
In 1856, the Treaty of Bayonne chose another way.
The island would belong to both countries, undivided.
Lawyers call that a condominium. Shared ownership, with no split.
That left one question. Who enforces the law on the island today?
In 1901, the two states signed a convention. Policing passes between them, in turns of six months.
Spain holds the duty from 1 February to 31 July.
France holds it from 1 August to 31 January.
Citizens of either country answer to their own courts. Anyone else answers to the country on duty.
Ownership stays shared. Only the duty moves.
Today, the island is closed to the public.
It is about 210 metres long and 40 wide. Nobody lives there.
A calendar replaced a line on a map. Lake Constance and the Moselle are shared too.
So who owns it?
Both countries. All year. Only the duty changes hands.
